source: Dhami et al. OSF project 'Alternative hypotheses evaluation' (osf.io/hcdp3) and child 'Technical Report' (osf.io/frcwn)
finding: Pulled the OSF project through its public API. The root project has no files. Its only child, 'Technical Report', holds two files: a Word report (Belton and Dhami, 2016) and a CSV of 64 rows. Neither is the 2024 layout study data.
numbers: Root node files: 0. Child frcwn files: 2 (docx, csv). Project created 2023-08-17, child created 2023-09-04.
limits: No layout condition variable in the CSV and no HypRow/HypCol/HypText cell counts anywhere on OSF. So the per-layout percentages (61.8/39.2/67.3) still cannot be checked from OSF.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 stays open. Do not cite the per-layout percentages as verified; cite only the text-level result (HypRow differs, chi2(2)=9.43, p=.009).

source: Belton and Dhami (2016) Technical Report: Development of an Alternative Hypotheses Evaluation Task Set
finding: The task set behind the 2024 study was first piloted in one matrix format (two hypotheses as columns, 12 evidence items as rows, which is the ACH-style layout, HypCol in 2024 terms). Task 1 is built so that confirm-only picks A while balanced or disconfirm-only picks B.
numbers: N=64 UK staff and students (mean age 25.3, 76.6% students, 50.8% female), paper and pencil, no time limit. Task 1: Hyp A consistent score 9 vs B 6, A inconsistent 10 vs B 4, net A -1, B +2. Choice: 48.4% chose A (confirm-only), 51.6% B. Task 2: 6.3% chose A, 93.8% B. Strategy: 47.6% CONS, 47.6% BAL, 4.8% INCONS. Self-report matched strategy for 75.9%; of CONS-classified people 59.3% said they used only consistent evidence.
limits: One format only, so it gives a baseline for the hypotheses-in-columns layout, not a layout contrast. Sample is 76.6% students.
agent_relevance: Baseline CONS rate for hypotheses-in-columns matrices in a separate sample is 47.6%, below the 61.8% derived for HypCol in 2024 (not verified). Both are near half or more, so the column matrix does not remove confirm-only choice. Use 45 to 60% as the human rate when we set up an agent test.

source: Belton and Dhami (2016) technical report data CSV (hyp task tech report data_.csv)
finding: Read the CSV locally. 64 participant rows, columns for the likelihood ratings, hypothesis choices, evidence usefulness ratings, a strategy code and the credibility tasks. There is no layout column.
numbers: Strategy code counts: code 3 (balanced) 30, code 1 (confirm-only) 30, code 2 (inconsistent-only) 3, one blank. Student/staff/other: 49 students, 9 staff, 6 other.
limits: Counts match the report (30/63 = 47.6%). The 2024 per-layout counts are not here.
agent_relevance: Confirms the 2016 numbers. The 2024 raw data must be requested from the authors if we want per-layout counts.

source: Belton and Dhami (2016) technical report, credibility tasks 3A/3B
finding: Credibility sensitivity in the single-matrix pilot: of those who chose A in task 3A, a share switched to B in 3B when told the evidence for A was low credibility.
numbers: All but 3 of 64 chose A in 3A. 67.2% of the rest switched to B in 3B (sensitive). In 2024 Study 1, 77/78/75% switched across layouts.
limits: Pilot is one layout; 2024 is three layouts. The 67.2 vs 75-78% gap may be sample or procedure.
agent_relevance: Sensitivity to credibility is a stable two-thirds to three-quarters in humans regardless of layout. Supports claim K03.

source: Jhaveri, GX-Chen, Sucholutsky, Choi (2026) Failing to Falsify: Evaluating and Mitigating Confirmation Bias in Language Models (NeurIPS 2026, arXiv 2604.02485v2)
finding: Eleven LLMs, thinking and non-thinking, play the Wason 2-4-6 rule-discovery game. All 11 favour confirming tests. The ratio of incompatible to compatible tests (I:C) correlates positively with task success, with a stronger trend in thinking models. This is the closest direct LLM test of confirm-only behaviour, but it is about choosing tests, not scoring a hypothesis-by-evidence table.
numbers: 11 LLMs (Gemini-2.5-Pro, Qwen3 8B/14B/32B thinking and non-thinking, QwQ-32B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-70B, GPT-4o and others). Task success from 6% to 78% within the turn limit. Interventions raise rule discovery from 42% to 56% on average. Under a controlled prior, Spearman rho 0.341, p=0.021 between I:C and success.
limits: Layout is not manipulated. Number triples, not intelligence evidence. Read from PDF text extraction; figure values not read.
agent_relevance: LLMs show confirm-only bias in test selection. This is a reason to build a disconfirming-test step, but it says nothing about rows vs columns. Gap 1 stays open.

source: Jhaveri et al. (2026) Failing to Falsify, interventions section
finding: Prompting interventions borrowed from human debiasing (Dual-Goal, Think-in-Opposites) reduce confirmation bias; distilling the intervention behaviour generalises to a Blicket-detector task and to math self-correction.
numbers: Dual-Goal improves task success in 8 of 11 model-inference setups. In the Blicket test, TiO raises both success and I:C on average for thinking models. Average rule discovery 42% to 56% (abstract).
limits: Gains are uneven across models (3 of 11 setups do not improve with Dual-Goal). Effects measured on synthetic rule tasks.
agent_relevance: A short instruction to look for incompatible tests is a cheap S4 element with measured gain on rule discovery. It is an instruction effect, not a layout effect.

source: Ngweta et al. (2025) Towards LLMs Robustness to Changes in Prompt Format Styles (Mixture of Formats)
finding: Using FormatSpread-style variants, giving each few-shot example a different format reduces the spread in many tasks. It does not test chain of thought or reasoning models.
numbers: Models: falcon-11B, Llama-2-13b (base and chat), llama-3-70b-instruct. 16 SuperNaturalInstructions tasks, 1,000 samples, 5 shots, 10 format variants. Llama-3-70B spreads (traditional vs MOF): task1347 0.276 vs 0.071, task1612 0.215 vs 0.064, task280 0.049 vs 0.020, task161 0.035 vs 0.037 (no gain). MOF mean accuracy is lower on some cells (falcon-11B task1612 0.553 vs 0.638).
limits: Older and small models only. No variance, CIs or significance tests reported. Chain of thought is listed as future work.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 partly open: this follow-up of FormatSpread does not answer it. Mixed formats in the examples only helps few-shot prompts, which our zero-shot schema does not use.

source: Romanou et al. (2026) Brittlebench: Quantifying LLM Robustness via Prompt Sensitivity (arXiv 2603.13285v4)
finding: Meaning-preserving prompt perturbations still hurt current frontier models. Chain of thought lifts accuracy but removes only a small part of the brittleness.
numbers: Average performance falls by up to 21%. One perturbation changes the relative model ranking in 63% of cases. Perturbations explain up to half of a model's performance variance. Models: GPT-5 (minimal thinking), Claude Opus 4.5, Llama 3.1/3.3, Qwen3. GPT-5 minimal thinking shows the largest absolute drops. Claude Opus 4.5 with CoT: accuracy drop under perturbation 2.79% to 2.38% (0.41 points, 17% relative).
limits: Perturbations are typos, stopword deletion, extra spaces, padding, paraphrase: not layout or table orientation. The CoT test used one model (Claude Opus 4.5), on word-level perturbations. Over 1,800 runs.
agent_relevance: Closest answer to gap 4: explicit reasoning does not remove prompt-surface sensitivity. Still measure the spread on our own S4 prompt, and report a range over formats, not one format.

source: Romanou et al. (2026) Brittlebench appendix H: mixed-effects test of CoT and brittleness
finding: Regression of per-question accuracy on CoT, perturbation and their interaction shows a small but significant interaction, so CoT mitigates brittleness a bit. Perturbations also lower the quality of the reasoning trace as judged by GPT-5, and better traces go with higher accuracy.
numbers: McNemar chi2=787.71, p<0.001 over 83,870 questions: CoT correct and non-CoT wrong on 3,413 (4.1%); reverse on 1,454 (1.7%). Interaction beta=.007, p=.006.
limits: Single frontier model; LLM judge for trace quality; answer extraction by regular expression.
agent_relevance: Reasoning is not a cure for format sensitivity. Supports keeping the S4 table in one fixed, tested serialization.

source: Ashury-Tahan et al. (2026) The Mighty ToRR: A Benchmark for Table Reasoning and Robustness (arXiv 2502.19412v3)
finding: Ten table datasets, many serializations (HTML, CSV, JSON, Markdown, indexed row major, DataFrame, concatenation) and perturbations such as row shuffle, column shuffle and transpose. No single format wins. Each example gets 35 scores from different prompt configurations and these vary widely.
numbers: Best absolute score about 0.50. Gap between best and weaker models is narrow. Kendall's W between model rankings from single prompt configurations is low. Going from 1 to 10 prompts raises W by more than 0.35. FinQA W rises from 0.35 to 0.93 with 11 prompts, NumericNLG from 0.29 to 0.54. Models include claude-3-5-sonnet, gpt-4o, gemini-1.5-pro, llama-3.1-405b, qwen2-72b.
limits: Tested models are 2024-era, no reasoning-mode models. Exact transposed-table drop not extracted.
agent_relevance: Confirms K08/K17: no universal best serialization. For S4 pick a serialization by testing a few on our own model. Row vs column orientation effects on reasoning models are still untested.

source: Veseli et al. (2025) Positional Biases Shift as Inputs Approach Context Window Limits (arXiv 2508.07479, COLM 2025)
finding: The lost-in-the-middle U-shape is strongest when the input fills up to about half the context window. Past that, the first-position advantage collapses and a distance-from-the-end bias takes over. Positional bias in reasoning mostly comes from retrieval: if retrieval succeeds, the position curve is much flatter.
numbers: 6 open models: Llama-3.1-70B, Llama-3.3-70B, Llama-3-70B, Mistral-Small-24B, Qwen-2.5-32B, Gemma-2-27B. 4 datasets (MonoRel, PIR, RuleTaker, BoxTracker), 100 instances each, 7 relative lengths 0.06 to 1.0 of context window. Retrieval success lifts reasoning accuracy: Qwen-2.5-32B 0.38 to 0.82, Llama-3.3-70B 0.35 to 0.74.
limits: No frontier closed or reasoning-mode models. Small samples (100 per dataset). The authors say inheritance is 'largely, though not entirely' true.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: a short S4 table sits far below half the window, where the middle dip is strongest. Put decisive evidence where we can, or restate it at the end, and test it.

source: Positional Failures in Long-Context LLMs (arXiv 2605.23170v1, 2026)
finding: Audit of 11 long-context benchmarks: none jointly controls task position, filler content and context length for reasoning. In a GSM8K position test, several current models lose a lot when the question moves from the end to the middle; others do not.
numbers: 9 models incl. DeepSeek-V3.2 (reasoning mode), Kimi K2.5/K2.6, GLM-5.1, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, MiMo-V2.5-Pro, Qwen2.5-7B. GSM8K middle minus end: Qwen 2.5-7B -86/-84/-94 points at 8K/32K/64K; MiMo-v2-Flash -12/-24/-88; DeepSeek-V3.2 no drop. Newer models with_solutions filler at 64K within 6 points except MiMo-V2.5-Pro -32. questions_only filler: drops 16 to 56 points. ARC 8K: 6 to 40 point drops, only Qwen significant after Bonferroni.
limits: N=50 per condition (95% CI about 14 points), one seed in most 64K cells, five API stacks (provider confound), preprint, filler type changes the result so it may be distraction not position.
agent_relevance: Closest 2026 data for gap 8: position sensitivity is model-specific and depends on filler. No direct test on a short S4 table. Needs a position-shuffle control in our bench.

source: Tian et al. (2025) Distance between Relevant Information Pieces Causes Bias in Long-Context LLMs (LongPiBench, ACL Findings 2025)
finding: Seen only in a search summary. Three commercial and six open models tested on multi-evidence tasks: most are robust to the classic lost-in-the-middle effect but show noticeable bias linked to the spacing between relevant pieces.
numbers: 3 commercial, 6 open-source models (counts from the summary; no scores read).
limits: Not opened. Summary only.
agent_relevance: Spacing between evidence items matters, not only position. In an S4 table, keep related evidence adjacent.

source: Schkade and Kleinmuntz (1994) Information displays and choice processes: differential effects of organization, form, and sequence (OBHDP 57(3):319-337)
finding: From abstract-level records only. Display organization (matrix or list), form (numbers or words) and sequence (sorted or random) each change how people pick, combine and weigh information. Organization mostly shaped how much information was acquired; form shaped combination and evaluation; sequence had a limited effect on acquisition.
numbers: 60 MBA students chose the best of 8 loan applications described on 4 attributes. Processes inferred from verbal protocols and decision times. Organization had the largest effect on effort. Self-reported effort did not track actual effort well.
limits: Full text not opened (paywalled). The matrix there is alternatives-by-attributes in multi-attribute choice, not evidence-for-hypothesis scoring. No row vs column hypothesis test.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 only partly closed. The principle (display changes which strategy is cheap) fits Dhami, but the originals do not predict row over column for hypotheses. Theory support only.

source: Kleinmuntz and Schkade (1993) Information displays and decision processes (Psychological Science 4(4):221-227)
finding: Abstract page opened. Argues that display features (form, organization, sequence) change the expected effort and accuracy of each strategy and so shift which strategy people choose. Cost-benefit framing.
numbers: No numbers on the abstract page; the article is behind a login.
limits: Abstract only. No data on alternative vs attribute organisation could be recorded.
agent_relevance: Gives a likely mechanism for a layout effect on confirm-only: the row layout makes whole-hypothesis comparison cheaper. A hypothesis to test, not a result.

source: Essay scoring under holistic and analytic prompts with open LLMs (arXiv 2604.00259, 2026)
finding: Closest data on holistic vs decomposed LLM judgments (gap 10). Agreement with humans is highest for a single holistic score and drops for trait-by-trait (analytic) scoring.
numbers: Llama 3.1 70B/405B/8B, GPT-OSS 120B/20B, zero-shot. QWK holistic ASAP 2.0: 0.533/0.601 (70B, keywords/guidelines prompts), GPT-OSS 120B 0.117/0.299. Analytic ELLIPSE: 0.321/0.235 (70B). DREsS: 0.414/0.394. On ELLIPSE, Cohesion QWK 0.566 but Grammar 0.203, Conventions 0.219; bias for low-level traits about -1.04 to -1.05. The paper wording is inconsistent on whether analytic is better on DREsS.
limits: Essay grading, not evidence evaluation. No dependency between traits. Open-weight models only.
agent_relevance: Weak support that per-item analytic scoring is not automatically better than holistic scoring. No test of cell-by-cell scoring for dependent evidence exists. Gap 10 stays open.

source: ACH-Grounding (suprathermal) open-source proposal, listed on sats4llms
finding: Seen only in a search summary. A project that has the LLM fill an evidence by hypothesis matrix (degree and direction of support per cell) while deterministic code computes the ranking. No measured results found.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Not opened. Not peer reviewed. Claims that ACH reduces confirmation bias in LLMs are untested.
agent_relevance: Same design as our S4 (LLM judges cells, code aggregates). Matches the design but gives no evidence it works; PRISM's +0.8 for the matrix is the only measurement.

source: Search log: replication and follow-ups of Dhami et al. (2024)
finding: Searched for a replication, a preregistered follow-up or an extension with non-student samples, and for LLM studies of rows vs columns and of sequential vs one-shot matrix filling. Found none. Dhami 2024 Study 2 (62 Dutch military analysts) used only the ACH-style layout, so it cannot test the row advantage.
numbers: Study 1 N=161 (HypCol 55, HypRow 51, HypText 55). Study 2 N=62, 66.1% BAL, 19.4% CONS. Zero replications found by web search on 2026-11-10 (a negative result, not proof of absence).
limits: Web search coverage is partial; a replication could be in a venue not indexed. Search budget was used up.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1, 2, 3 stay open. The row-layout claim stays single-source.

source: Tabular robustness papers: arXiv 2406.12719 (robustness of LMs for tabular QA) and arXiv 2512.00947 (Table as a Modality)
finding: Seen only in search summaries. Transposing a table hurts answer accuracy; instruction-tuned models cope better. A 2025 paper argues existing serializations lose structure and answers are not permutation-robust; it proposes a hypergraph encoding (TAMO).
numbers: TAMO: up to 42.65% average gain over baselines on 5 datasets (summary figure only).
limits: Not opened; numbers are from summaries. Older models.
agent_relevance: Supports the NORM idea (gap 7): a step that puts the table in a standard orientation is plausible. Still no test with reasoning models on evidence matrices.

source: Search log: FormatSpread on reasoning models and chain of thought (gap 4)
finding: Searched for FormatSpread-style spread on reasoning-mode models. No study measures spread with thinking on vs off across many formats. Nearest: Brittlebench (typos and spacing, not layout) and PHYBench (robustness gains from reasoning come partly from compensatory strategies).
numbers: Brittlebench: CoT cuts the perturbation drop by 17% relative. PHYBench: DeepSeek-R1 39 vs 97 original on one perturbation type, o1-preview 15 vs 94 (search summary only).
limits: Negative search; PHYBench numbers seen in snippet only.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 stays largely open. Treat format spread as unknown for reasoning models and measure it.
